extracted.intended_audience: farmers, rural homeowners, builders, public-health officers, and students of hygiene
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for selecting the location, orientation, and soil/site conditions for rural houses to promote hygiene, reduce disease risk, and improve comfort and efficiency of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid low, swampy, marshy ground and stagnant ponds
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate neighborhood of low, swampy, marshy ground, of stagnant ponds, or of sluggish streams should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such locations are objectionable chiefly because they provide breeding places for insects (e.g., mosquitoes) and can produce effluvia and nuisance odors; they also encourage damp cellars and discomfort even if dampness alone does not directly cause the listed infectious diseases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid land subject to inundation (flood-prone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Low land, subject to inundation, even though this may happen only occasionally, is not a wise choice of a building site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Floods produce exposure and inevitable effluvia after waters recede; historical example cited: village inundation in New York State, 1889.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid streams carrying organic matter or sewage
rubrics_metrics.description: The vicinity of a stream carrying organic matter, such as sewage from a town above, should undoubtedly be avoided on account of possible odors in summer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owner testimony: windows had to be kept shut at night because of effluvia from a distant stream carrying city sewage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deep and narrow valleys because of reduced sunlight
rubrics_metrics.description: A deep and narrow valley should be avoided, not so much because of possible dampness, but because of the noticeably lessened amount of sunlight which such a location involves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morning sun comes up much later and afternoon sun disappears earlier in such valleys; sunlight is described as 'the best foe to disease,' so lack of sunlight reduces healthfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hilltop exposure to strong cold winds; prefer gentle south-facing slopes or knolls
rubrics_metrics.description: The top of a hill exposes a house to strong and cold winds, not desirable on any account, and involving large expense for heating; sloping ground, therefore, facing the south if possible, or better, some knoll which rises above the general surface of a southern slope, affords an ideal location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A south or southeast/southwest-facing slope keeps off north winds and captures winter sun while avoiding excessive wind exposure and heating costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orient house to maximize sunlight on all sides
rubrics_metrics.description: If the house itself faces due south, the windows on the north have no sunlight. If, on the other hand, the house faces southeast or southwest, then all sides of the house will receive direct sunlight at some time of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer orientations that allow sunlight into multiple sides to improve health and reduce dampness and mold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep trees at a distance so they do not block sun or damage roof
rubrics_metrics.description: Trees are useful for shade and as a wind screen, but a thick growth directly over a shingle roof allows organic matter to accumulate so that vegetation develops and the roof decays more rapidly; trees near enough for leaves to drop on the roof will stop rain troughs and leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trees should be far enough away from the house to allow the sun to enter the windows freely and to keep away from the roof objectionable animals (e.g., squirrels) that may infest attics and walls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient space between houses and from the highway
rubrics_metrics.description: It is highly desirable that a house should be built so as to leave as much land under control between the buildings and the lot line as possible; have a reasonable space between a house and the highway to keep road dust from the house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In villages where wells and privies/cesspools are used, proximity can create health hazards (a neighbor's later-built cesspool can ruin a well). A front yard of at least fifty feet depth is advised when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of sidehill sites with horizontal subsoil strata and upstream cesspools
rubrics_metrics.description: The location on a sidehill, even when otherwise advantageous, is to be regarded with suspicion if the subsoil strata are horizontal and neighbors up the slope have cesspools in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaching through rock or soil from upstream cesspools may cause continual dampness in lower cellars and contaminate water—inspect subsoil and neighbors' waste disposal before choosing such sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid damp cellars for comfort and indirect health reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: A damp cellar means conditions favorable to the development of mildew and rot; prevents vegetables from keeping a normal length of time; accounts for moldy, decaying odors throughout the house, and is generally disagreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While dampness alone is not held to directly induce the specific infectious diseases discussed, it causes discomfort and may reduce inhabitants' vitality, possibly increasing susceptibility to disease; therefore select dry house sites and construct dry cellars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize sunlight as a key health factor for the dwelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Since sunlight is the best foe to disease, the more sunlight enters a house, the healthier are those who live in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Site selection, orientation, and avoidance of tree/shade obstructions should be made with the aim of maximizing sunlight exposure, especially winter sun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider soil composition when choosing building site
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular form which mineral elements assume in soil (sand, sandstone, clay, shale, limestone, etc.) is of interest in choosing a location for a house, for reasons including drainage, water quality, and tendency to marsh formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soil indirectly affects health via drainage and water-supply quality; no absolute scientific rule for 'fitness' of soil exists, but different soils have characteristic advantages and drawbacks (see specific soil types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer granite, sandstone, gravel, and sand (with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Localities where granite rock abounds and comes near the surface are usually healthy because the surface slope carries off drainage rapidly; sandstone, being porous, may be considered a healthy foundation; gravel has always been assumed to be the healthiest soil on which a house could be built; sand is equally desirable except where vegetable matter has been mixed with the sand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gravel is ideal provided ground water reaches its highest stage three or four feet below the cellar bottom. Watch sands mixed with vegetable matter—water from such sands may contain nitrates causing vegetable overgrowth and possible laxative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid limestone areas and clays/heavy alluvial soils where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Limestone rock is commonly laid down in horizontal strata and while it may give rapid slopes, marshes are very common; the drinking water is to be suspected because it is hard and cavities/seams can transmit pollutants. Clays and heavy alluvial soils are not usually considered desirable on which to build because they hold moisture and marshes are apt to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limestone areas may produce hard water and allow long-distance travel of polluting material through seams; clays retain moisture, increasing dampness and marsh risk—both raise sanitary concerns for wells and foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider topography's indirect effects on disease patterns (including cancer observations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Soil and topography affect health indirectly because different rock types produce different surface formations; regions of water-soaked valleys and certain topographies (e.g., clay subsoil with thin surface) have been associated with abnormally high cancer mortality in parts of Europe and some New York State districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While causation is not established, be cautious about building in regions noted for persistent marshy valleys and poor drainage; note historical epidemiological observations linking topography and disease patterns pending scientific clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small towns and villages with water supplies but lacking sewerage pose high typhoid risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest danger from typhoid fever is neither in the country nor the large city, but in the village or small city where growth and congestion have made necessary the introduction of a water-supply, and in many cases this has not been supplemented by the construction of a sewerage system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground becomes saturated with filth, percolating into wells; introduction of the typhoid germ from outside can start widespread epidemics. Effective organization of local health boards and proper sewerage are essential to reduce risk.
